script.title: Target Costing: price first, cost next
script.caption_hook: The market sets your price. So who sets your cost?

lines.say: Ma'am, why does the market decide my product's cost?
Because customers pay the price. So we start with price, then fix cost. That's target costing.
But normally we add profit to cost, right?
Yes, traditional costing is cost plus profit equals price. Target costing reverses it.
Okay, can you give a simple example?
Say a phone. Customers will pay only ₹10,000. That's the target selling price.
And our profit? We can't work for free!
Right. Target cost equals target selling price minus target profit. Say you want 20% profit on sales.

board.title: Target Cost
board.sub: TSP = selling price, TP = target profit

lines.say: Exactly. ₹10,000 minus ₹2,000, so target cost is ₹8,000.
But what if our design costs ₹8,500 now?
Then cost gap is estimated cost minus target cost: ₹500. Value engineering must close it.
So the gap is a loss?
Not yet. It's the cost cut still needed. Price stays fixed, because the market sets it.
Remember: price minus profit equals permitted cost. Price is fixed, cost must bend!

check_notes: Writer: Example: price ₹10,000, 20% profit on sales = ₹2,000, target cost ₹8,000, estimated ₹8,500, gap ₹500. Per unit assumed (a phone). Word count about 160.

Checker: Line 14 (voice): 'Not yet' suggests the gap will turn into a loss. It won't: at ₹8,500 the phone still earns ₹1,500, which is ₹500 below the ₹2,000 target profit. Better: 'No. It's a shortfall against target profit, the cost cut still needed. At ₹8,500 you still earn ₹1,500, just not the ₹2,000 target.'
Checker: Line 8 board sub: 'TSP = selling price' should say 'TSP = target selling price', so it matches the voice line and the abbreviation.
Checker: Line 12 (voice): 'Value engineering must close it' makes VE sound like the only tool. Better: 'Value engineering (with tools such as kaizen and design changes) is used to close it.'
Checker: Line 4 board: the red cross on 'Old way' suggests cost-plus is wrong. It's a different approach, not an error. A neutral icon would be better (wording/visual only).
